name: Polaris
distance_baseline: Approximate stellar distance from Earth. The Sun is only 1 AU from Earth, so at 433 light-years the Earth and Sun distances are effectively the same.
notes: North Star; useful for navigation because it sits near the north celestial pole.

sky_position.note: Always 46° above the northern horizon from Goldendale — never rises or sets. Find it by following the two outer stars of the Big Dipper's bowl straight toward the North.

name: Arcturus
distance_baseline: Approximate stellar distance from Earth. The Sun is only 1 AU from Earth, so at 36.7 light-years the Earth and Sun distances are effectively the same.
notes: A bright orange giant star and one of the easiest stars to spot in spring and summer.

sky_position.note: Brilliant orange star high in the SE — the brightest star in the northern half of the sky. Hard to miss. Follow the arc of the Big Dipper's handle to find it.

name: Vega
distance_baseline: Approximate stellar distance from Earth. The Sun is only 1 AU from Earth, so at 25 light-years the Earth and Sun distances are effectively the same.
notes: Very bright blue-white star in the Summer Triangle.

sky_position.note: Bright blue-white star rising in the ENE. Gets much higher by midnight. One corner of the Summer Triangle.

name: Venus
distance_baseline: Average orbital-radius baseline, not a live telescope ephemeris. Earth distance is approximated as |1.000 AU - 0.723 AU| = 0.277 AU; Sun distance uses Venus's average orbital radius of 0.723 AU.
notes: Included in this list as requested; Venus is a planet, not a star.

sky_position.note: Brilliant morning star low in the east before sunrise. Unmistakable — the brightest thing in the pre-dawn sky besides the Moon.

name: Cassiopeia
distance_baseline: Rough representative distance using Caph, one of Cassiopeia's nearest bright stars. The whole constellation spans multiple distances, so this is an anchor value rather than one exact distance.
notes: Constellation (not a single star). Distance shown is a rough distance to one of its nearest bright stars (Caph).

sky_position.note: Low in the north, close to the horizon. The W-shape is harder to see at this height. Gets higher and easier in the autumn sky.

name: Big Dipper
distance_baseline: Rough representative distance using Mizar, one of the bright stars in the Big Dipper. The full asterism spans multiple star distances, so this is a simple anchor value.
notes: Asterism (not a full constellation). Distance shown is a rough distance to one of its nearest bright stars (Mizar).

sky_position.note: Almost directly overhead, tilted toward the NW. The most prominent star pattern in the May sky — the hardest thing in the sky NOT to find.

name: Little Dipper
distance_baseline: Rough representative distance using Kochab, one of the bright stars in the Little Dipper. The full asterism spans multiple star distances, so this is a simple anchor value.
notes: Asterism (not a full constellation). Distance shown is a rough distance to one of its nearest bright stars (Kochab).

sky_position.note: High in the north, circling around Polaris. Much fainter than the Big Dipper. Polaris marks the very tip of its handle.
